title.title: Memory–sample lower bounds for noiseless regression
title.subtitle: Claim: a streaming learner with $A d^2$ bits needs $\Omega_A(d \log(1/\varepsilon))$ exact Gaussian measurements

plain: Learning from exact measurements with limited memory: below a threshold, you pay for it with extra data

beats.text: Recover a unit vector from exact measurements $y = \langle x, s \rangle$, one pass
With room for the normal equations, about $d$ measurements suffice
Claimed: with only $A d^2$ bits you pay the extra $\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and that is tight

steps: At the end, success means the guess hits a tiny target
Walk the learner backward, one block of samples at a time
Each block widens the target by only a fixed factor
So reaching a fair chance takes many blocks

after.label: Claimed, 27 Sep 2026
after.note: noiseless, $A d^2$ bits; matches the upper bound

achievement.note: A narrow model: noiseless Gaussian design, uniform prior, finite-state learner

verify.detail: Eight Lean files across six overlapping papers; a few variant statements left out
verify.ourCheck: We did not build the Lean or referee the proof

voice.text: With d squared bits, d samples solve regression. With less memory, what does it cost?
Walking back block by block, each block helps only a fixed amount.
Claimed: an extra log factor is unavoidable.

sources.quote: a streaming learner retaining at most A d^2 bits between exact Gaussian linear measurements y=<x,s> needs Omega_A(d log(1/eps)) measurements
Sharan-Sidford-Valiant (STOC 2019) 'Memory-sample tradeoffs for linear regression with small error': with <= d^2/4 bits
sharpening Sharan, Sidford and Valiant's $\Omega(d\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$-type bound
the summary's claim is narrow (noiseless, Gaussian design, uniform prior, finite-state learner)
Matches the natural O(d log 1/eps)-sample low-memory upper bound
With d^2 bits you can store the normal equations and solve regression from d samples
